title: Locks and Deadlocks
description: Compare-and-swap primitives, spinlock vs mutex tradeoffs, readers-writer locks, deadlock detection with wait-for graphs, lock ordering, and a real production deadlock postmortem.

segments.text: Locks are the most common synchronization primitive, and they're responsible for more production incidents than almost any other concurrency mechanism. Understanding when to use a spinlock versus a mutex, and how deadlocks form and are detected, is essential knowledge for any staff-level engineer.

At the hardware level, locks are built on compare-and-swap, or CAS. The CPU atomically compares a memory location to an expected value and, if they match, writes a new value. This single instruction is the foundation of all lock-free and lock-based concurrent data structures. On x86, it's the CMPXCHG instruction, taking roughly 10 to 50 nanoseconds.

A spinlock loops on CAS until the lock is available. The thread stays on the CPU, burning cycles. This sounds wasteful, but for very short critical sections — under one microsecond — it's faster than a mutex because you avoid the overhead of a kernel context switch. Linux kernel code uses spinlocks extensively for this reason.

A mutex puts the thread to sleep when the lock is contended, waking it when the lock becomes available. The context switch costs one to five microseconds, but the sleeping thread doesn't burn CPU. For critical sections longer than a few microseconds, mutexes win. Most application-level locks should be mutexes. Modern implementations like futex combine both: spin briefly, then sleep.

Readers-writer locks allow multiple concurrent readers but exclusive writers. When reads vastly outnumber writes — like a configuration cache — this dramatically reduces contention. But writer starvation is a risk: continuous readers can prevent writers from ever acquiring the lock. Most implementations use writer-preferring policy to prevent starvation.

Deadlock requires four conditions simultaneously: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, and circular wait. Thread A holds lock one and waits for lock two. Thread B holds lock two and waits for lock one. Both wait forever. In production, deadlocks manifest as hung requests, growing thread pools, and eventual service unresponsiveness.
segments.thought_prompt: Of the four deadlock conditions, which one is easiest to eliminate in practice?

segments.text: The most practical deadlock prevention technique is lock ordering. Assign a global order to all locks and always acquire them in ascending order. If every thread acquires lock one before lock two, circular wait is impossible. In database systems, InnoDB uses lock ordering on table IDs. In application code, sort resource IDs before acquiring their locks.

Deadlock detection uses a wait-for graph. Each thread is a node. An edge from A to B means A is waiting for a lock held by B. A cycle in this graph is a deadlock. PostgreSQL builds this graph every second and aborts one transaction in the cycle. MySQL InnoDB checks on every lock wait, making detection faster but more expensive.

Lock timeout is deadlock detection's simpler cousin. If a thread can't acquire a lock within a timeout, it gives up and retries. PostgreSQL's lock_timeout and Java's tryLock with timeout implement this. The downside: false positives. A slow but legitimate lock holder gets its transaction aborted by an impatient waiter.

Real postmortem: a payment service deadlocked under load. The transfer function locked the sender account then the receiver account. Two simultaneous transfers between the same two users — A to B and B to A — created a cycle. Fix: always lock the account with the lower ID first, regardless of transfer direction. Deployed in 15 minutes, ended a two-hour outage.

Deadlocks get harder in distributed systems. Service A calls service B while holding a lock. Service B calls service A while holding its own lock. You've created a distributed deadlock that no single system can detect. This is why distributed lock services like Redlock have timeouts built in and why you should minimize cross-service lock dependencies.
segments.thought_prompt: How would you redesign a system to eliminate cross-service lock dependencies entirely?

segments.text: Use spinlocks for sub-microsecond critical sections, mutexes for everything else. Prefer readers-writer locks when reads dominate. Prevent deadlocks with lock ordering. Detect them with wait-for graphs or timeouts. And always design for the failure case: what happens when your lock times out? The answer should be retry with backoff, not crash.
